newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy June yr/yr CPI seen bottoming out.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy June yr/yr CPI seen bottoming out.

text.p: Italian yearly consumer price inflation is seen bottoming out in June around May's level although some analysts forecast CPI ticking up to mark the start of an upward trend until the year end, a Reuter poll showed.
The 13 economists surveyed on average saw a rise in June month-on-month inflation of 0.2 percent and a year-on-year rate of 1.5/1.6 percent, but one forecast a rate of 1.8 percent.
In May, CPI rose a monthly 0.3 percent to give a yearly rate of 1.6 percent, a 28-year low but at the top end of market expectations which had been for a rate of 1.5 or 1.6 percent.
In June 1996, prices rose 0.2 percent month-on-month and 3.9 percent year-on-year.

Italy's 11 sample cities are due to publish their preliminary June CPI data either side of the coming weekend. On Friday, Milan, Genoa, Trieste, Florence and Bari issue their figures while on Monday it is the turn of Turin, Venice, Bologna, Perugia, Naples and Palermo.
The final national figures will be published on July 4.
Lucia Trevisan of Caboto, which sees a 0.1 percent monthly rise and annual rate of 1.5 percent, noted petrol pump prices had risen slightly at end-May only to fall shortly afterwards.
Cariplo, also seeing 0.1 and 1.5 percent, said it did not think food prices would have an inflationary effect this month.
But Banco di Sardegna said in a market comment it reckoned that CPI data this month "should conclude the long cycle of falls begun way back in November 1995."
Indeed, the analysts who forecast an upturn mainly attributed it to higher food prices particularly due to a hike in prices of coffee and fruit and vegetables.
Furthermore, the recent outbreak of swine fever in the Netherlands "has pushed down pork meat prices but caused other meat prices to rise," said Giovanni Polastri of 4CAST.
San Paolo Bank in London was among the more pessimistic forecasters, seeing a monthly rise of 0.3 percent and 1.8 percent for the year.

It said that wage rises would put pressure on the CPI data, and "with the increase in productivity being limited by the unfavourable position of the economic cycle, we believe we will see pressure on prices from June onwards."
"Also, prices of food products and clothing are usually at their highest in summer and the impact of both should start to be seen from June," San Paolo added.
